query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, the intrinsic hardness and strength are primarily governed by lattice distortions arising from atomic size mismatch. These distortions impede dislocation motion by increasing local energy barriers, thereby elevating yield strength and hardness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic single‐phase HEA produced via controlled casting/solidification (ensuring a homogeneous, disordered BCC or FCC solid solution) with a conventional mix of multiple principal elements.
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the alloy composition to vary the atomic size mismatch while keeping other factors (valence electron concentration, processing history, phase stability) constant. For example, replace one constituent with an element of similar chemical behavior but a distinctly different atomic radius.
generation.conditions: Testing should be conducted at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures (below ≈800 °C) on as-cast or homogenized samples to ensure that the microstructure remains a single-phase solid solution, where dislocation glide governs deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion, measurable by the spread in interatomic distances (e.g., via XRD peak broadening or pair distribution function analysis).
generation.mechanism: Increased atomic size disparity produces a strongly distorted lattice, which serves to pin dislocations by raising the local activation barriers for slip. This pinning reduces dislocation mobility, thereby increasing both hardness and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs engineered to have a higher degree of lattice distortion (i.e. larger atomic size mismatch) will exhibit statistically higher hardness and tensile yield strength compared to otherwise similar alloys with reduced lattice distortion, with analogous ductility in the same single-phase framework.
generation.baseline: A control HEA composition with minimal atomic size variance, resulting in a relatively uniform lattice and lower resistance to dislocation motion.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in single-phase, well-homogenized HEAs where precipitation or ordering effects are minimal. At very high temperatures, or when multi-phase or recrystallized microstructures form, other mechanisms (e.g., diffusion‐controlled processes) may obscure the lattice distortion effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between atomic size mismatch and strengthening, as well as possible interactions with secondary strengthening mechanisms (such as precipitation) or grain boundary effects, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of HEA samples: one set with a high degree of atomic size mismatch and another with reduced mismatch achieved by selecting constituent elements with more similar atomic radii (while preserving similar valence and processing conditions). Ensure both series are processed identically to yield homogeneous single-phase microstructures. Evaluate the lattice distortion using X-ray diffraction and/or pair distribution analysis, and then perform microindentation hardness tests and tensile tests.
measurements: XRD peak broadening and/or pair distribution function to quantify lattice distortion
Tensile yield strength and ductility measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with higher calculated atomic size mismatch (and thus greater lattice distortion) do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength compared to the control series, or if the trend is reversed, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion is the primary mediator governing hardness and strength is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5.
